replay.q: Can I merge Gemma, Qwen and Kokoro into one network?
replay.a: No. They have different architectures and jobs. You build a system: several specialist models behind one gateway with one API.
Fine-tuning shapes behaviour. It teaches a model your formats, tone, tools, domain knowledge and local context.
No. Fine-tuning shapes behaviour; it does not add the broad reasoning of a model trained at frontier scale. Pick the strongest base you can host, then specialise it.

replay.q: What decides the quality of a fine-tuned model?
replay.a: Data quality decides the result. The dataset is the difference between a demo and a product: what you collected, how you cleaned it and how you measured it.

replay.q: What should I check before collecting data?
replay.a: Check the licence of every dataset and base model. Use open licensed data, data you own, data with user consent, and keep a provenance record for every source.

replay.q: Can I train on outputs from a commercial AI?
replay.a: Usually not. Many commercial AI providers forbid using their model outputs to train competing models. Use outputs only from models whose licence allows it.

replay.q: What is the architecture of the stack?
replay.a: One gateway, many specialists. Clients call an API gateway, a router picks the model, and specialists handle chat, code, vision, speech, images and embeddings.
The gateway gives one API with keys, quotas, logs, retries and fallbacks. LiteLLM proxy or your own FastAPI gateway can do it.
The router picks the model by task: chat, code, an image in the request or audio in the request. Start with rules and add a small classifier later.
vLLM serves language and vision models on GPU with fast batched inference and an OpenAI-style API.

replay.q: What should I use for small or edge models?
replay.a: Use llama.cpp or Ollama for small, edge or CPU models.
Use Whisper or faster-whisper for speech to text, and Kokoro for text to speech, with streaming.

replay.q: Is the robot face a neural network?
replay.a: No. The face is a renderer, not a model. The LLM emits structured emotion events, and Rive, Lottie, WebGL or Unity animates them.

replay.q: Which tools are used for ops?
replay.a: Use Docker, Prometheus and Grafana to deploy and monitor. Add Kubernetes later.

replay.q: How do I choose a base model?
replay.a: Start with one strong general model of about 8B to 32B. Add specialists only when measurements show a gap.
Prefer Apache-2.0 or MIT licences if developers will build commercial products on your work.
Mixture-of-Experts models have few active parameters per token, so inference is faster and fine-tuning is cheaper.
No. Public leaderboards do not predict your tasks. Always compare the base model on your own test set.

replay.q: Which models suit chat and reasoning?
replay.a: Evaluate the Qwen 3.x family, Gemma 4, Mistral Small or Ministral 3, and DeepSeek, which is large and needs many GPUs.

replay.q: What matters most for a coding agent model?
replay.a: Pick a model with native tool calling. Agent behaviour matters more than raw code completion.

replay.q: Which vision model should I use?
replay.a: Use a natively multimodal model like multimodal Gemma or a Qwen-VL class model. They fine-tune more simply than bolting on an encoder.

replay.q: Which embedding models should I use?
replay.a: Use BGE, E5 or GTE class models for retrieval over developer docs.

replay.q: Which image models should I use?
replay.a: Use open diffusion models of the SDXL or FLUX class. Licences differ and some restrict commercial use, so read before you ship.
Kokoro 82M is a small text to speech model with Apache weights. It runs on CPU or a small GPU, and it is built for inference.

replay.q: How much of the project should go to data?
replay.a: Plan to spend about 60 to 70 percent of the whole project on data.

replay.q: What beats a large noisy dataset?
replay.a: No. A small, clean, well-labelled dataset beats a large noisy one.
Build the evaluation set first and keep it sealed. It tells you what data you actually need. Never train on it.

replay.q: How many examples should I write by hand?
replay.a: Write 20 to 50 example conversations by hand for each capability. They become your style guide and seed data.

replay.q: What goes in a provenance table?
replay.a: One row for every source: name and URL, licence, date and version, consent status, whether it contains personal data, and share-alike or attribution duties.

replay.q: Where can I get chat data?
replay.a: Tulu 3 SFT mixture, SmolTalk, OpenAssistant and FineWeb-Edu are starting points, plus real questions from your users with consent. Verify each licence.

replay.q: Where can I get code data?
replay.a: The Stack v2, licence-filtered GitHub repos and Stack Exchange dumps, plus your own repos and recorded terminal sessions.

replay.q: Where can I get speech data?
replay.a: Mozilla Common Voice, FLEURS and LibriSpeech, plus speakers from your region recorded with signed consent and transcripts.
Common Voice includes Ugandan languages and public models are weakest there. A few hundred hours of clean local speech can beat a much larger general model on your users.

replay.q: What are the stages of the cleaning pipeline?
replay.a: Extract, normalise, language ID, heuristic filters, exact dedupe, near-duplicate removal, quality scoring, PII scrub, safety filter, decontaminate, format, then split and version.

replay.q: What if one stage removes half the data?
replay.a: Stop and look at samples. If one stage removes 50 percent, either the source or the filter is wrong.

replay.q: How do I remove near duplicates?
replay.a: Use MinHash plus LSH on 5-grams, with a similarity threshold around 0.8. Duplicates cause memorisation and inflate scores.

replay.q: What does the PII stage remove?
replay.a: Remove emails, phone numbers, national IDs, addresses, API keys, passwords and tokens. Use regex plus Presidio, and gitleaks for code. Replace them with placeholders.
It removes any record that overlaps your evaluation set or public benchmarks, using n-gram overlap. Otherwise scores lie.

replay.q: How should I split my data?
replay.a: Split by source or conversation, never by random row, to prevent leakage. Then version it with DVC or Hugging Face datasets and write a data card.

replay.q: What happens with a wrong chat template?
replay.a: Wrong templates silently ruin fine-tunes. Convert to the exact chat template of the base model and print one tokenised example to check.
Manual review, dedupe report, distribution check, format check, safety and PII scans, and a written data card.

replay.q: How many rows should I read by hand?
replay.a: Read at least 200 random rows per source and per capability, and judge 95 percent or more acceptable.

replay.q: How much data do I need for style and format?
replay.a: Start with 1,000 to 10,000 high-quality examples. Quality dominates, and hundreds can already shift behaviour.

replay.q: How do I clean code data?
replay.a: Execute, do not just read. Run code and unit tests in a sandbox and keep only samples that pass. Remove secrets, generated files and destructive commands.

replay.q: How do I prepare speech for Whisper?
replay.a: Convert to 16 kHz mono WAV, normalise loudness, and cut segments of about 5 to 30 seconds with voice activity detection.

replay.q: How much audio does a new TTS voice need?
replay.a: 10 to 50 hours of clean audio is the usual range for good single-voice quality. Never train on a voice without written consent.

replay.q: How much data for emotion labels?
replay.a: Create 2,000 to 10,000 labelled lines covering greetings, thinking, errors, celebration, confusion, empathy and long explanations. Measure agreement between two labellers.
Lip-sync comes from TTS phoneme or word timing, not from the LLM.
LoRA trains small adapter matrices on top of a frozen base model. It is the default choice: cheap, fast, and it keeps base ability.
QLoRA trains LoRA adapters on a 4-bit base, so it needs much less GPU memory.
SFT trains on input to ideal output pairs. Use it to teach format, tone, tools and domain skills.
DPO trains on chosen versus rejected answers. Use it to polish helpfulness, safety and style after SFT.
GRPO is RL with verifiable rewards. It rewards answers that pass tests or checks, so it suits code, terminal agents, maths and tool success.
In distillation a student model learns from the outputs of a stronger teacher. Check the licence of the teacher first.

replay.q: Should I do a full fine-tune?
replay.a: Only with large data and many GPUs. It is usually unnecessary, so use LoRA by default.

replay.q: Should I try RAG before fine-tuning?
replay.a: Try prompting and RAG first. Retrieval gives the model documents at request time, and it is right when facts change often.

replay.q: Should I fine-tune to add facts?
replay.a: No. Use retrieval for changing facts, and fine-tune for skills and style.

replay.q: What is the best LoRA learning rate?
replay.a: Use 1e-4 to 2e-4 for LoRA, and about 10 times lower for full fine-tuning.

replay.q: What LoRA rank should I use?
replay.a: Use a rank of 16 to 64, with alpha equal to rank or 2 times rank.

replay.q: How many epochs should I train?
replay.a: Train 1 to 3 epochs, and stop when validation loss stops improving.

replay.q: What batch size should I use?
replay.a: Use an effective batch size of 32 to 128 sequences through gradient accumulation.
Mix 10 to 30 percent general data into training so the model does not forget. If general scores fall, add replay data or lower the learning rate or rank.
Train on assistant tokens only. Mask the loss on user tokens and tool outputs.
Run a tiny overfit test first: 20 examples, many steps. If the model cannot memorise them, the template, masking or learning rate is wrong.
Use bf16 compute with 4-bit base weights for QLoRA.

replay.q: How much GPU memory does an 8B model need?
replay.a: A 7B to 14B model needs 16 to 24 GB to fine-tune with QLoRA, and 8 to 20 GB to serve at 4-bit to 8-bit.

replay.q: How much GPU memory does a 32B model need?
replay.a: A 27B to 35B model needs 24 to 48 GB to fine-tune and 20 to 40 GB to serve.
Rent GPUs by the hour for training from RunPod, Lambda, Vast.ai or a hyperscaler, then keep a smaller always-on set for serving.

replay.q: Which tools are used for fine-tuning?
replay.a: Unsloth is fast with low VRAM on one GPU. LLaMA-Factory has a web UI, TRL with PEFT is the code-level stack, and Axolotl runs YAML recipes on many GPUs.

replay.q: How does a terminal agent work?
replay.a: A terminal agent is a loop: read the situation, choose a command or edit, run it, read the result, and continue.

replay.q: How do I keep a terminal agent safe?
replay.a: Sandbox it. Use Docker or gVisor isolation, timeouts, a command allowlist, confirmation for destructive actions, and audit logs.
Keep only trajectories whose tests or checks pass, plus a small set of recovery examples where the first command fails and the next one fixes it.

replay.q: What is the reward for an agent?
replay.a: Reward means tests pass, a minimal diff, and no forbidden commands. This step gives the biggest gain for agents.
Freeze the vision encoder first, and train LoRA on the language layers and the projector with image and text instruction data.

replay.q: How do I evaluate speech to text?
replay.a: Measure word error rate on a speaker-disjoint test set, per accent and per noise condition.

replay.q: How do I serve Whisper fast?
replay.a: Serve with faster-whisper, using CTranslate2, and add streaming with VAD chunking.

replay.q: What creates the movie feel in animation?
replay.a: Idle animation, blinking, micro-movements and easing curves create the movie feel, not the AI model.

replay.q: How do I train an image style?
replay.a: Train a LoRA from 50 to 500 curated, captioned, rights-cleared images. Serve on a dedicated GPU queue because generation is slow compared to chat.

replay.q: How many training rounds are best?
replay.a: Two or three rounds beat one big run. Collect failures, write better answers, add them, and retrain.

replay.q: What is the recommended way to combine models?
replay.a: Start with one multimodal model plus LoRA adapters for language, vision and code. Use separate models for Whisper, Kokoro, diffusion and embeddings.
vLLM multi-LoRA serves chat, code and persona adapters on one loaded base. It is cheap, because one set of base weights stays in memory.
Merge fine-tunes of the same base with mergekit: TIES, DARE or SLERP. It needs the same architecture, and you must test for regressions.
Audio goes to speech to text, an image goes to the vision model, the route /code goes to the coder, and everything else goes to chat.
It adds a small classifier to choose between fast and strong models: easy questions go to the small model and hard ones to the large model.
If a backend times out, retry on another replica or a smaller model, so the service degrades instead of failing.
Copy the OpenAI-compatible routes: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/audio/transcriptions, /v1/audio/speech, /v1/images/generations, /v1/embeddings and /v1/models.
Every existing SDK and tool then works with your gateway by changing only the base URL. This is the single biggest adoption decision you will make.

replay.q: How do I make serving fast?
replay.a: Use quantisation, continuous batching with paged KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding, MoE models, streaming and shorter prompts.
Quantisation with FP8, AWQ, GPTQ or GGUF roughly halves memory or better and raises tokens per second. Always re-run your eval on the quantised model.
Prefix caching reuses system prompts and long shared context, so there is less work per request.
A small draft model proposes tokens and the big model verifies them, which gives faster generation.
The first token or first audio chunk arrives sooner, so it feels much faster.

replay.q: What is the latency budget for a talking robot?
replay.a: Target under about one second to first sound: VAD 50 to 200 ms, speech to text 150 to 300 ms, LLM 150 to 400 ms, TTS 100 to 250 ms, network 50 to 100 ms.

replay.q: How do I deploy the stack?
replay.a: Start on one GPU server with Docker Compose: vLLM, gateway, Whisper, Kokoro, Redis and Postgres. Put nginx or Caddy in front with TLS and require API keys.
Keep a small quantised model through llama.cpp so the service degrades instead of failing.
Build images in CI and roll out new model versions behind a canary percentage, watching the numbers before going wider.
Never expose raw model ports. Sandbox the terminal agent, store secrets in a vault, and log without storing sensitive prompts unless users opt in.
Evaluation is not the last step. You build it first, run it after every change, and refuse to ship when it regresses.

replay.q: What should I compare a fine-tune against?
replay.a: Compare every candidate against the base model and against the previous version. Fine-tuning that does not beat the base is wasted.

replay.q: What should a golden prompt set contain?
replay.a: Use 200 to 500 golden prompts from real users, rated on a rubric.

replay.q: Can I trust an LLM judge?
replay.a: It is useful and cheap, but calibrate it: check its scores against human ratings on 100 samples.
Run jailbreaks, prompt injection through documents and web pages, harmful requests and privacy leaks.

replay.q: What should I measure for the whole system?
replay.a: Measure p50 and p95 latency, throughput, error rate and GPU cost per 1,000 requests, and load test at 2 times expected traffic.
Weights in safetensors, quantised builds, a clear licence, a model card, a data card, Docker images and a one-command start script.
A model card states intended use, training data summary, evaluation results, known limits and safety notes.
An OpenAI-compatible API, Python and JavaScript SDKs, a quickstart that works in five minutes, a playground, an API reference and a public changelog.

replay.q: What is the best future training data?
replay.a: Collect opt-in feedback. Corrected answers are your best future training data. Review failures weekly and retrain monthly or quarterly.
Publish honest benchmarks including weak areas. Developers trust that.

replay.q: How long does the roadmap take?
replay.a: The roadmap takes 12 weeks: gateway and baselines, clean data, agent harness, LoRA, speech and face, DPO and GRPO, safety and load tests, then the v1.0 launch.
